# Adad: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Adad** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Hymn to Adad.** The Akkadian Hymn to Adad describes the god's arrival in the storm: the heavens thunder, the earth shakes, and his lightning flashes from one horizon to the other.  He rides the storm winds; the mountains tremble before him.  When Adad speaks in thunder, both gods and mortals listen.

**Adad in the Deluge.** In the Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI, Utnapištim recounts the great flood: 'The gods of the abyss rose up; Nergal tore out the dam's bolt; Ninurta marched on and made the weirs overflow. ' Adad's voice is the storm within the deluge; his thunder is the signal that the divine council has unleashed destruction upon the land.  The storm god who brings rain in due season here becomes the agent of cosmic cleansing.

**Adad of Aleppo and Royal Treaty.** At Aleppo (Halab), the West Semitic storm god Addu was one of the most powerful deities of the Bronze Age Levant.  The great kings of Mari, Yamkhad, and Hatti invoked him in treaties and royal correspondence; his thunder guaranteed oaths and his absence meant disaster.  In the Middle Assyrian period Adad appears beside Aššur as a national god, granting the king victory in the field as surely as he granted rain to the field.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves


## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Adad
- **ASCII form:** adad
- **Meaning:** "The thunderer"
- **Domain of influence:** Storm, Thunder
- **Pantheon:** Mesopotamian
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒅎
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 5 of 542

## The Name Travels

The Sumerian storm god Iškur and the Akkadian Adad were identified with one another from an early date; in bilingual texts and god lists they function as a single deity with two names.  In the West Semitic world he was Addu or Hadad, a major god of Aleppo and the Syrian steppe, and his imagery influenced the Canaanite storm-god Baal.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Adad** stands at [/adad/](/adad/) — [lore](/adad/lore/), [scholars](/adad/scholars/), [patterns](/adad/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.
